questions.subject: Reading
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish supported details, contradicted details and details absent from the passage.
questions.passage:
In a fictional trial at a market in Enugu, traders complained that the covered walkway flooded after a short storm. Investigators initially blamed a narrow drain under the entrance. When they watched a storm from the upper floor of a nearby building, they saw water from three roofs reach the entrance at almost the same moment. They decided to test whether delaying one stream of water could reduce the peak flow.

At the western end of the market, the team redirected one roof pipe into a shallow planted bed. A gravel layer created spaces in which water could gather before it reached an outlet. The outlet still led to the original drain. The team left the other two roof pipes alone, so their flow continued along the usual route. A measuring stick was installed at the entrance to record the highest water level reached during each storm.

The largest reduction occurred during a storm that followed several dry days. When storms arrived close together, the planted bed was less effective because it had not emptied completely. The record contained no storms severe enough to overflow the bed. The investigators therefore proposed testing the design through a longer rainy season before recommending it to other markets.

Several traders had expected the bed to keep the entrance dry. The trial team clarified that it had aimed to lower the highest water level, even if water still briefly covered the walkway. To help explain the distinction, it drew two graphs of water depth over time. One graph had a lower peak than the other, although both showed some flooding.
questions.prompt:
Before watching a storm, investigators suspected the drain beneath the entrance.

Answer TRUE if the text supports the statement, FALSE if it contradicts it, or NOT GIVEN if it does neither.
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph says the narrow entrance drain was their initial explanation.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a writer’s position from its contradiction and from claims the writer does not address.
questions.passage:
Libraries sometimes compare shelves by counting the number of loans each metre of shelf generates. As a way to notice a change in borrowing, this measure is useful. As the sole basis for deciding what to keep, however, it mistakes one visible action for the whole purpose of a collection. A repair manual may stay in the building because readers consult a single page before returning to their work. A little-read local directory may matter chiefly because few other libraries have preserved it.

My objection is not to counting. Without records, librarians can easily mistake a crowded room for evidence that every service in it is thriving. In a small fictional branch, staff began using return trays for books consulted inside the building. The trays revealed that a shelf of job application guides attracted readers who rarely took copies home. This observation supported a decision to keep the guides within easy reach. It did not reveal whether those readers found work.

There is a further danger in replacing one measure with a much longer list. Recording every visit to every shelf could absorb staff time without answering any pressing question. A sensible approach is to begin with a decision that actually needs making, then collect the smallest amount of evidence likely to improve it. If the issue is where to put a collection, observing where people look may matter more than learning what they think of the authors.

Finally, there are decisions for which counting can never settle the question. A branch may decide that documenting the life of its neighbourhood is part of its duty. Evidence can guide how the archive is used or preserved, but a low tally of visits cannot, by itself, determine whether the duty should exist.
questions.prompt:
The writer considers loans per metre useful for detecting shifts in borrowing.

Answer YES if the statement agrees with the writer, NO if it contradicts the writer, or NOT GIVEN if the writer takes no position on it.
questions.explanation: The writer explicitly accepts the measure for noticing borrowing changes.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish supported details, contradicted details and details absent from the passage.
questions.passage:
A fictional planning class in Ibadan compared two ways of walking to a bus stop. One route was shorter and followed a broad road. The other wound through narrow streets beside houses and walls. A map made the shorter route seem the obvious choice. The class wanted to know whether the time spent in direct sunlight would tell a different story.

Pairs of students walked both routes at the same steady pace shortly after midday. Each student carried a paper map and marked the start and end of every shaded stretch. The pairs compared notes at the bus stop. They had agreed that a patch counted only if it shaded the width of the pavement. This rule excluded thin shadows cast by signs, even if they cooled part of a walker’s arm.

On the broad road, most shade came from trees. On the narrow route, much came from buildings. The narrow route took longer to walk but involved less time in direct sunlight at midday. When the class repeated the walk late in the afternoon, the difference was smaller. Shadows from the buildings had moved, opening parts of the narrow route to the sun while covering some stretches that had been exposed earlier.

The students drew a map showing which parts of each route were shaded on both walks. One participant suggested printing a permanent sign recommending the narrow streets. The class decided to leave the recommendation off the map. Its measurements had been made on a single day and under one set of street conditions. Instead, the map showed the starting times so users could see exactly when the observations applied. The exercise had compared exposure, not how comfortable different walkers felt.
questions.prompt:
The students walked both routes at the same pace during their midday comparison.

Answer TRUE if the text supports the statement, FALSE if it contradicts it, or NOT GIVEN if it does neither.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that the pairs used the same steady pace on both routes.
